name: Fish Farming (Aquaculture) Basics
objectives: Given your water, land, money and local market, choose tilapia or African catfish and a pond or tank system, giving at least three reasons linked to your site and buyers

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a species and a system
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose tilapia or African catfish and a pond or tank system for your farm.
This lesson builds toward: Given your water, land, money and local market, you will choose tilapia or African catfish and a pond or tank system, giving at least three reasons linked to your site and buyers.
Two fish are farmed most in Africa. Nile tilapia is popular in Ghana, Kenya, Côte d'Ivoire and Egypt. It eats pellets and the natural food in green water, and it is sold fresh, fried or grilled. Mixed-sex tilapia breed in the pond and fill it with small fish, so farmers buy mono-sex (mostly male) fingerlings. Improved strains such as GIFT grow faster; WorldFish reports farmers in Nigeria reaching about 600 g in six months with GIFT and good feeding.
African catfish (Clarias) is the main farmed fish in Nigeria and is popular fresh and smoked. It can breathe air, so it survives low oxygen better and can be kept more densely, often in tanks. But it needs more protein-rich feed, and bigger fish eat smaller ones, so you sort them by size.
Choose the system: an earthen pond is cheap to run where soil holds water; a lined pond or concrete or plastic tank works on sandy soil or small plots but costs more to build and needs more water changes. Most important: before you choose, ask buyers which fish and what size they want, and at what price.
Step by step:
- Ask three buyers (market sellers, hotels, smokers) which fish, size and price they want.
- Check your water: how much, all year, and how clean.
- Check your soil: does it hold water?
- Choose the species buyers want and your water can support.
- Choose pond or tank by soil, space and money.
Words to know:
- Aquaculture: farming fish and other water animals.
- Fingerling: a young fish, about finger size, bought for stocking.
- Mono-sex: fingerlings that are nearly all one sex (male tilapia), so they grow instead of breeding.
- GIFT: Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia, a faster-growing tilapia strain developed by WorldFish.
Official sources:
- WorldFish: GIFT tilapia farming in Nigeria (hatcheries, growth, markets), 2025
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
Try it now: Ask at least three buyers near you which fish they want, at what size and price. Write down their answers, then choose tilapia or catfish and a pond or tank, with three reasons from your site and your buyers.
You can now choose between tilapia and African catfish, and between a pond and a tank, using your water, soil and buyers.

check.q: Why do tilapia farmers buy mono-sex fingerlings?
options: So the fish grow instead of breeding and filling the pond with small fish
check.why: Mixed-sex tilapia breed in the pond and end up stunted and small.

check.q: Your soil is sandy and does not hold water. Which system fits best?
options: A pond on the river bank
A lined pond or a tank
check.why: A liner or tank holds water where the soil will not.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Siting and building a pond, and permits
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a pond site and list the permits to ask about.
This lesson builds toward: Given a possible site, you will check the site for water, soil, slope and flooding and list the permits to ask about, naming the fisheries body in your country you will contact.
A good pond site has: water all year, clean and not polluted by factories, mines or sprayed fields; soil with enough clay to hold water (squeeze a damp handful: if it keeps its shape, that is a good sign); a gentle slope so the pond can fill and drain by gravity; no flooding; and is close enough to watch against thieves and predators.
Build the pond with a firm, sloped dike (bank) planted with grass to stop erosion, an inlet with a screen so wild fish cannot get in, and an outlet or drain pipe so you can empty the pond for harvest. A pond of a few hundred square metres is easy to manage for a beginner. Fence it if you can, and keep animals and children away. Prepare the pond before stocking: dry it, remove mud and wild fish, and lime and fertilise it if your extension officer advises.
Fish farms often need registration or a permit, and sometimes a water-use or environmental approval. In Kenya, the Fisheries Management and Development Act, 2016 requires aquaculture to be registered and licensed with the Kenya Fisheries Service. In Ghana, the Fisheries Commission issues aquaculture permits. In Nigeria, ask the Federal Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture and your state ministry; in Côte d'Ivoire, the ministry in charge of fisheries. Some areas allow only certain species or strains. Rules change, so check before you dig.
Step by step:
- Check the water source: enough all year, and clean.
- Do the squeeze test on the soil; ask an extension officer to confirm.
- Choose gently sloping land above flood level, near where you can watch it.
- Plan a firm dike, a screened inlet and an outlet to drain.
- Contact the fisheries office: registration, permits, water use, allowed species.
- Prepare the pond before stocking, as your extension officer advises.
Words to know:
- Dike: the earth bank around a pond.
- Inlet and outlet: the pipes or channels where water comes into and leaves the pond.
- Permit: official permission you need before you start or run the farm.
Official sources:
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
- Kenya: Fisheries Management and Development Act, 2016 (registration and licensing of aquaculture), on FAOLEX
- Fisheries Commission (Ghana): permits and licences, including aquaculture
Try it now: Walk your possible site. Write down the water source, the result of the soil squeeze test, the slope, any flood risk and how you will guard it. Then find the phone number or office of your fisheries body and list three questions to ask about permits and species.
You can now judge whether a site suits a fish pond, plan its main parts and know which fisheries office to ask about permits.

check.q: You squeeze damp soil and it keeps its shape. What does this suggest?
options: The soil has clay and may hold water
check.why: Clay soil that holds its shape usually holds pond water; ask an extension officer to confirm.

check.q: Before digging a fish pond in Ghana, whom should you check with about permits?
options: Nobody; fish ponds need no permits
check.why: Ghana's Fisheries Commission issues aquaculture permits.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Water quality with simple tests
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Test pond water and act when it goes wrong.
This lesson builds toward: With a thermometer, pH strips and a Secchi disk, you will test pond water and say what to do when oxygen, temperature or pH is out of range, recording each test with the date and time.
Fish live in the water, so bad water kills them fast. Watch three things. Oxygen: in green ponds it is highest in the afternoon and lowest at dawn, because plants and algae use oxygen at night. Cloudy days, too much algae, rotting feed and manure make it worse. An FAO paper notes tilapia become much less active when oxygen falls to about 1 to 2 mg per litre. Temperature: tilapia and catfish are warm-water fish; they eat and grow slowly in cool water, such as in highland areas or the cold season. pH (how acid the water is): water that is too acid or too alkaline stresses fish.
Simple tests: a thermometer for temperature; pH paper strips or a kit; a Secchi disk (a white-and-black plate on a marked stick) to see how green the water is; and your eyes at dawn. Fish gasping at the surface at dawn mean oxygen is low. If you can afford one, an oxygen test kit or meter gives a number.
If oxygen is low: stop or cut feeding until the fish recover, add fresh water, splash or pump water to mix in air, and remove dead fish. If the water is very green, fertilise less. If pH is wrong, ask your extension officer about liming. Record every test with the date and time.
Step by step:
- Check the pond at dawn: are fish gasping at the surface?
- Take the water temperature with a thermometer.
- Test pH with strips or a kit once a week.
- Push the Secchi disk down until it disappears; note the depth.
- Low oxygen: stop feeding, add fresh water, splash or aerate, remove dead fish.
- Write every result with the date and time.
Words to know:
- Dissolved oxygen: oxygen mixed in water, which fish breathe through their gills.
- pH: a number that shows how acid or alkaline water is.
- Secchi disk: a black-and-white plate lowered into water to see how clear or green it is.
- Aeration: mixing air into water, with a pump, paddle or by splashing.
Official sources:
- FAO, African Regional Aquaculture Centre (Kutty, 1987): dissolved oxygen in fish ponds
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
Try it now: Make a Secchi disk from a white plate painted with two black quarters, tied to a stick marked every 5 cm. Then make a water-test record sheet with columns for date, time, temperature, pH, Secchi depth, fish behaviour and action taken, and fill in one line from a pond or water source near you.
You can now check oxygen, temperature, pH and greenness with simple tools and act quickly when the water goes wrong.

check.q: When is oxygen usually lowest in a green fish pond?
check.why: At night plants and algae use oxygen and make none, so it falls until dawn.

check.q: At dawn you see fish gasping at the surface. What do you do first?
options: Stop feeding, add fresh water and splash or aerate
check.why: Gasping means low oxygen; less feed and more fresh, mixed water bring it back up.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Quality fingerlings and stocking density
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Work out how many fingerlings to stock and check a hatchery.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pond or tank size, you will work out how many fingerlings to stock and list checks for a certified hatchery, with the arithmetic correct and the density agreed with an extension officer or hatchery.
Good fingerlings are half the battle. Buy from a hatchery that is registered or certified by your fisheries authority, or recommended by your extension officer. Ask: Are the tilapia mono-sex, and which strain? Are the fingerlings all about the same size? How many die in the first weeks, and do they replace them? Can you see the hatchery? Healthy fingerlings swim actively, have no wounds, and are even in size. Wild-caught or mixed-size fish bring disease, breeding and cannibalism.
Stocking density is the number of fish per square metre (ponds) or per cubic metre (tanks). Too many fish means low oxygen, slow growth and small fish. A study of tilapia ponds in Côte d'Ivoire fed only with fertiliser found that 2 to 3 fish per square metre already reduced yield. With good pellet feed, more fish can be stocked, and tanks with water flow or aeration more again, especially for catfish. Agree your density with your extension officer or hatchery for your system.
Example (figures are only an example): a 20 m by 15 m pond is 300 square metres. At an example density of 3 fish per square metre, you stock 900 fingerlings. Move fingerlings in the cool of the morning, in oxygenated bags or clean water, and let the bags float in the pond for a while so the temperatures match before releasing them.
Step by step:
- Measure the pond: length x width = area in square metres.
- Agree a density with your extension officer or hatchery.
- Area x density = number of fingerlings.
- Choose a registered or recommended hatchery; ask about strain, mono-sex, size and losses.
- Check the fingerlings: active, no wounds, even size.
- Transport in the cool morning; float bags to match temperature before release.
Words to know:
- Stocking density: the number of fish per square metre of pond, or per cubic metre of tank water.
- Hatchery: a farm that breeds fish and raises young fish to sell.
- Cannibalism: fish eating other fish of their own kind, common in catfish of mixed sizes.
Official sources:
- Aquatic Living Resources (2001): high stocking densities reduce Nile tilapia yield in Côte d'Ivoire ponds
- WorldFish: GIFT tilapia farming in Nigeria (hatcheries, growth, markets), 2025
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
Try it now: Measure your pond or tank (or use 20 m by 15 m). Ask an extension officer or hatchery for a density for your system, and work out how many fingerlings to buy. Then write five questions to ask the hatchery before you pay.
You can now work out the number of fingerlings for a pond and choose a hatchery that sells quality fish.

check.q: A pond is 25 m by 10 m and the agreed density is 2 fish per square metre. How many fingerlings?
check.why: 25 x 10 = 250 square metres, and 250 x 2 = 500 fingerlings.

check.q: Which batch of catfish fingerlings should you refuse?
check.why: Mixed sizes lead to cannibalism, as bigger catfish eat smaller ones.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Feeding, feed conversion and common problems
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the feed conversion ratio and spot problems early.
This lesson builds toward: Given feed records and sample weights, you will calculate the feed conversion ratio and spot common problems early, correct to one decimal place.
Feed is usually the biggest cost in fish farming. Use a good-quality feed of the right pellet size for the fish's mouth; floating pellets let you see how much is eaten. Feed at the same times each day, and give only what the fish eat in a few minutes; uneaten feed rots and uses up oxygen. The amount rises as fish grow: every two to four weeks, net and weigh a sample of fish, work out the average weight, and adjust feed using the feed maker's or extension officer's chart. Store feed dry and off the floor; mouldy feed is poison.
The feed conversion ratio (FCR) shows how well feed turns into fish: FCR = feed given / weight gained. Example: you fed 400 kg and the fish gained 250 kg, so FCR = 400 / 250 = 1.6. A lower FCR means less feed per kg of fish. FCR goes up with overfeeding, poor feed, bad water and sick fish.
Common problems: low oxygen at dawn; predators such as birds, snakes and otters, and thieves; tilapia breeding when fingerlings were mixed-sex; catfish eating each other when sizes differ (sort them); floods washing fish out; and disease. Signs of sick fish are not eating, sores, odd swimming or many deaths. Remove dead fish, stop feeding, check the water, and call your fisheries extension officer or a vet; do not use drugs or chemicals without their advice.
Step by step:
- Feed good-quality feed of the right size at fixed times.
- Give only what the fish eat in a few minutes.
- Every 2 to 4 weeks, weigh a sample and adjust feed by the chart.
- Record all feed given.
- FCR = feed given / weight gained.
- Watch daily for problems; call the extension officer or vet for sick fish.
Words to know:
- Feed conversion ratio (FCR): kilograms of feed used to grow one kilogram of fish.
- Sample weighing: netting and weighing some fish to find their average weight.
- Predator: an animal that eats fish, such as some birds, snakes and otters.
Official sources:
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
- FAO, African Regional Aquaculture Centre (Kutty, 1987): dissolved oxygen in fish ponds
Try it now: Make a feeding record with columns for date, feed given (kg), sample average weight and notes. Then work out the FCR for this example: 300 kg of feed given, fish gained 200 kg. Write one way to lower it.
You can now feed fish well, calculate the FCR and spot common problems early.

check.q: You fed 450 kg of feed and the fish gained 300 kg. What is the FCR?
Why should you give only what fish eat in a few minutes?
options: Uneaten feed rots, uses up oxygen and wastes money
It makes the water clearer for swimming
check.why: Uneaten feed is wasted money and pollutes the water.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Harvesting, selling and the economics of one cycle
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a costed plan for one cycle with the profit and break-even price.
This lesson builds toward: Given costs, expected survival, harvest weight and price, you will write a costed plan for one cycle with profit and break-even price, with every cost included and the sums correct.
Plan the sale before you stock. Agree with buyers on the size, the day and the price, and harvest in the cool morning. Stop feeding a day before so the fish travel better. Drain the pond part way and net the fish, or drain it fully for a complete harvest. Keep fish cool and clean on ice or in shade, and sell fast: fresh fish spoils within hours in the heat. Smoking or drying, common for catfish in Nigeria, adds value and time to sell. Partial harvests of the biggest fish can spread sales over several weeks.
Cost one cycle on paper first. Example for a 300 square metre tilapia pond in Ghana (all figures are examples only; use your own quotes): 900 fingerlings at GHS 1.50 = GHS 1,350; feed: expected harvest 720 fish (80% survival) x 0.35 kg = 252 kg, and at an expected FCR of 1.6 that needs about 400 kg of feed at GHS 12 = GHS 4,800; pond preparation GHS 300; labour and security GHS 1,200; harvest and transport GHS 300. Total costs GHS 7,950.
Sales: 252 kg at GHS 40 per kg = GHS 10,080. Profit = 10,080 - 7,950 = GHS 2,130. Break-even price = total costs / kg harvested = 7,950 / 252 = about GHS 31.50 per kg. If the buyer's price is near your break-even, change the plan: better fingerlings, less feed waste, or a better buyer.
Step by step:
- Agree size, day and price with buyers before stocking.
- List every cost: fingerlings, feed, pond preparation, labour, security, harvest, transport.
- Expected harvest = fingerlings x survival x harvest weight.
- Feed needed = weight gained x expected FCR.
- Profit = sales - total costs.
- Break-even price = total costs / kg harvested.
Words to know:
- Survival rate: the share of stocked fish still alive at harvest.
- Break-even price: the price per kg at which sales just cover all costs.
- Partial harvest: taking out the biggest fish and leaving the rest to grow.
Official sources:
- Farmers' manual on small-scale tilapia pond farming in Ghana (Agyakwah et al., 2020; CGIAR repository)
- WorldFish: GIFT tilapia farming in Nigeria (hatcheries, growth, markets), 2025
Try it now: Final task: write a costed plan for one cycle of your own pond or tank (or the example): species, site and permit checked, water tests, fingerlings and hatchery, expected survival, harvest weight and feed, every cost, expected sales, profit and break-even price per kg.
You can now plan a harvest and sale and work out the profit and break-even price of one fish farming cycle.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Species and site No reason given for the species, or no buyer asked. Species and system chosen with three reasons from the site and buyers. Names the buyers, the size they want and the price they quoted. Site and permits Site not checked or no fisheries body named. Water, soil, slope and flooding checked; the fisheries body and permit questions listed. Has contacted the fisheries office and notes the answer. Water quality plan No water tests in the plan. Dawn checks, temperature, pH and Secchi tests with how often and what to do when out of range. Includes a filled-in test record and an emergency plan for low oxygen. Fingerlings and stocking Number of fingerlings missing or wrong, or no hatchery named. Correct number from area and agreed density; a registered or recommended hatchery named with checks. Notes the strain, mono-sex status and the hatchery's replacement policy. Costs, profit and break-even Costs missing, feed not linked to FCR, or sums wrong. All costs, feed from expected gain x FCR, profit and break-even price correct. Shows a second case with lower survival or a lower price, and what the farmer would do. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Total costs are NGN 900,000 and you expect to harvest 600 kg of catfish. What is the break-even price?
When should you agree the sale with buyers?
options: After harvest, when the fish are on ice
Before stocking, and confirm before harvest
Only if fish are left over
check.why: Fresh fish spoils quickly; a buyer agreed early avoids forced cheap sales.
